name: Ninja
baseline: GNU Make (CMake Unix Makefiles generator backend)
workload: Meson author's experiment: 1000 generated trivial C files (each defining one function and including a header) built into one executable with CMake, once with its Make backend and once with its Ninja backend, four parallel processes, fastest of several runs; plus an anecdote about no-op builds of the Clang compiler.
claimed_speedup: Switching the CMake backend from Make to Ninja shaves 3.5 seconds (over 20%) off the total build time of the 1000-file project with no CMake file changes. Anecdote on the same page: no-op build times of 30 seconds for Make versus less than one second for Ninja when compiling the Clang compiler. The bar-chart values are images, so only these two text figures are quotable.
hardware: 2011-era MacBook Pro running Ubuntu 13.04 (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Deliberately has no build-file features (no conditionals, no built-in rules, no globbing); build.ninja files are meant to be emitted by a generator such as CMake or Meson, so Ninja alone is not a replacement for a hand-written Makefile. It needs a generator step. Uses all hardware threads by default; the manual says the design trades convenience for speed.
caveats: The only quantified third-party comparison reachable is written by the author of Meson, a competing build system, and is old (2011 hardware, Ubuntu 13.04); CPU model, GNU Make version, compiler and flags are not stated, the generator script is not on the page, and the per-build-system numbers are in images that were not readable here. The 30 s versus under 1 s Clang figure is explicitly anecdotal. First-party claim on the Ninja manual page (https://github.com/ninja-build/ninja/blob/master/doc/manual.asciidoc, introduction): Chromium, with over 30,000 source files, had other build systems, including one built from custom non-recursive Makefiles, that took ten seconds to start building after changing one file, while Ninja takes under a second; no hardware, date or method is given there, so it is tier C on its own. The CMake Best Practices lead for this project gives no timing for Ninja. Ninja's advantage is mostly incremental and no-op startup time; clean full builds are compiler-bound, and the 20 percent gain is on a synthetic project of trivial files, so real projects will see less on clean builds.

name: clcache
baseline: uncached MSVC compile (cl.exe without a compiler cache)
workload: OpenMW GitLab CI job (MSBuild, MSVC 2022, 64-bit RelWithDebInfo) run uncached versus with a third-party fork of clcache and a CI-restored cache across successive pipeline runs.
claimed_speedup: Merge request text: the average uncached MSBuild RelWithDebInfo job is either barely passing or barely failing the 2 hour timeout; with the clcache fork the 2nd build (partial cache) succeeded in 100 minutes, the 3rd build (full cache) in 55 minutes, and subsequent jobs in as little as 49 minutes. Roughly 2.2x (120 / 55, derived from page data, the 120 minute figure being the job timeout, not a measured uncached time).
compiler_and_flags: MSVC 2022, 64-bit, RelWithDebInfo; clcache with CLCACHE_COMPRESS, cache limit 1.5 GB (clcache -M 1610612736)
tradeoffs: Python wrapper around cl.exe (the repo also has a pyinstaller folder) that stores compiler output in a local directory cache; the optional clcachesrv.py server is documented as greatly improving the performance of cache hits. Upstream is archived: Python 3.10+ and MSVC 2019+ patches live only in forks, which is why users run forks. Precompiled-header caching is not available upstream (the OpenMW fork author says his fork has experimental changes toward it).
caveats: The README and CHANGELOG of frerich/clcache carry no timing numbers (only 'greatly improves performance of cache hits' for the server). The only reachable numbers are third-party CI anecdotes. The OpenMW merge request (opened 2025-11-29) used Aussiemon's fork pinned to a commit, not upstream, and states no uncached time (only that it is near the 2 hour timeout), no runner hardware, and mixes cache states across different pipeline runs, so the speedup is approximate and not a controlled comparison. The upstream issue https://github.com/frerich/clcache/issues/251 (2016, Windows Server 2012 R2, E5-2650) reports the opposite: a 5 to 8 minute build rose to 23 minutes with a cold cache and was roughly equal to no clcache when fully cached, blamed on cache lock contention and virus scanning. The same MR author found ccache's MSVC precompiled-header hits as slow as misses and called clcache the most stable option, but wished ccache could match its speed.
found_via: seed-record pass; started from https://github.com/frerich/clcache (book lead: Software Architecture with C++, 2nd ed., ch. 7), then WebSearch for clcache build times, upstream issue #251 and the OpenMW merge request.

name: sccache
workload: CI lint job of the amplihack-rs repository: cargo build (dev profile) that also compiles the C/C++ library lbug through cmake, run uncached on main, then with sccache on first and repeated runs, using GitHub Actions cache storage.
claimed_speedup: Cargo build step 17 min 26 s uncached, 6 min 23 s on the first sccache run (C/C++ 1,803 hits and 319 misses, 85 percent; Rust 10 hits and 223 misses, 4 percent) and 2 min 46 s on the rerun; whole Lint and Format job 1,425 s uncached versus 711 s and 478 s. About 2.7x then 6.3x on the cargo build step (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: cargo build, dev profile; C/C++ built through cmake (compiler version not stated)
tradeoffs: ccache-like wrapper with a client/server model and many storage backends (local disk, S3, GCS, Azure, Redis, Memcached, WebDAV, GitHub Actions cache); caches C, C++, CUDA and Rust; also offers icecream-style distributed compilation with authentication. Needs a background server process and cache storage configuration.
caveats: Neither the sccache README nor docs carry timing numbers. The reachable figures are one third-party CI pull request (opened and merged 2026-10-16) with a mixed Rust plus C++ workload, no runner hardware, compiler or sccache version stated, 219 sccache write errors from GitHub cache throttling, and the uncached run being a different pipeline run than the cached ones; the gain comes mostly from C/C++ objects already cached on main. Against ccache, the only measurement found is the repo's own issue https://github.com/mozilla/sccache/issues/160 (2017, Firefox clobber build with Clang 4.0.0 on Ubuntu 17.04, hardware not stated), where fully cached ccache took 35 s wall versus 107 s wall for sccache's local disk cache (3 to 4.5 times slower); the issue was closed in February 2024 as 'should be good now' without new measurements, so sccache has no evidence of beating ccache here.
found_via: seed-record pass; started from https://github.com/mozilla/sccache (book lead: Software Architecture with C++, 2nd ed., ch. 7), then WebSearch for sccache C++ build times, issue #160 and amplihack-rs PR #1571.
